claim: A one-tailed Wilcoxon sign-rank test rejected the null hypothesis that the PDMI is not > 0.
source: A one-tailed Wilcoxon sign-rank test rejected the null hypothesis that the PDMI is not > 0, supporting the conclusion that low-frequency laser stimulation impaired orientation discrimination.
evidence: The claim is supported by the results of a statistical hypothesis test (Wilcoxon sign-rank test) applied to the experimental data.

claim: Low-frequency laser stimulation impaired orientation discrimination.
source: A one-tailed Wilcoxon sign-rank test rejected the null hypothesis that the PDMI is not > 0, supporting the conclusion that low-frequency laser stimulation impaired orientation discrimination.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Wilcoxon sign-rank test) of experimental data showing PDMI > 0.

claim: High-frequency stimulation did not impair orientation discrimination.
source: Applying the same test to data collected (a) during high-frequency stimulation or (b) when the monkey performed the task on stimuli appearing away from the opsin site, we find no evidence of impairment, supporting our original conclusion that the impairment is limited to low-frequency stimulation and is spatially specific to the retinotopic location of the opsin site.
evidence: The claim is supported by Wilcoxon sign-rank test results showing no significant effect during high-frequency stimulation.

claim: The impairment is spatially specific to the retinotopic location of the opsin site.
source: Applying the same test to data collected (a) during high-frequency stimulation or (b) when the monkey performed the task on stimuli appearing away from the opsin site, we find no evidence of impairment, supporting our original conclusion that the impairment is limited to low-frequency stimulation and is spatially specific to the retinotopic location of the opsin site.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical tests showing impairment at the opsin site but not away from it.

claim: The Weibull function is more widely used in the psychophysical literature than the logistic function.
source: It is more widely used in the psychophysical literature due, in part, to the fact that the threshold parameter (alpha) in the Weibull function is decoupled from the other parameters (slope, guessing rate).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about psychophysical methods in the field.

claim: The threshold parameter (alpha) in the Weibull function is decoupled from the other parameters (slope, guessing rate).
source: It is more widely used in the psychophysical literature due, in part, to the fact that the threshold parameter (alpha) in the Weibull function is decoupled from the other parameters (slope, guessing rate).
evidence: The claim describes a mathematical property of the Weibull function, which is established knowledge in psychophysics, and is cited to Nachmias, 1981.

claim: The shape of the Weibull function depends only on the slope and the guessing rate.
source: In other words, the shape of the Weibull depends only on the slope and the guessing rate.
evidence: The claim describes a mathematical property of the Weibull function based on established knowledge.

claim: Varying the threshold parameter, alpha, shifts the Weibull function along the x-axis without changing its shape.
source: Varying the threshold parameter, alpha, shifts the function along the x-axis without changing its shape.
evidence: The claim describes a mathematical property of the Weibull function based on established knowledge.

claim: The decoupling of parameters in the Weibull function enables independent estimates of the threshold and slope (Nachmias, 1981).
source: This decoupling therefore enables independent estimates of the threshold and slope (Nachmias, 1981).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nachmias, 1981.

claim: The logistic function does not decouple threshold and slope parameters.
source: The logistic function, though similar in shape, does not decouple these parameters.
evidence: The claim describes a mathematical property of the logistic function based on established knowledge.

claim: The PDMI distribution calculated using Weibull fits is non-normal according to the Lilliefors test.
source: After recalculating the PDMI values using Weibull fits we find that the PDMI distribution continues to be non-normal (Lilliefors test) so we again applied the Wilcoxon sign-rank test.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical test results (Lilliefors test) performed on the recalculated PDMI data.

claim: Low-frequency stimulation (but not high-frequency stimulation) impairs perception.
source: Thus, these analyses support the main conclusions of the paper — that low-frequency stimulation (but not high-frequency stimulation) impairs perception and that this effect is specific to the opsin site.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the statistical analyses showing significant impairment with low-frequency but not high-frequency stimulation.

claim: The perceptual impairment effect is specific to the opsin site.
source: Thus, these analyses support the main conclusions of the paper — that low-frequency stimulation (but not high-frequency stimulation) impairs perception and that this effect is specific to the opsin site.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the statistical analyses showing impairment at the opsin site but not at the non-opsin site.

claim: The Estimation Statistics approach provides a richer representation of the data than the Null-Hypothesis Significance Testing (NHST) approach.
source: This approach, which has been widely adopted in some scientific disciplines, provides a richer representation of the data than the more commonly used Null-Hypothesis Significance Testing (NHST) approach and is being adopted as a new standard in some neuroscience journals (Bernard, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bernard, 2019, and represents established knowledge in statistical methodology.

claim: Estimation Statistics is being adopted as a new standard in some neuroscience journals (Bernard, 2019).
source: This approach, which has been widely adopted in some scientific disciplines, provides a richer representation of the data than the more commonly used Null-Hypothesis Significance Testing (NHST) approach and is being adopted as a new standard in some neuroscience journals (Bernard, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bernard, 2019.

claim: The Estimation Statistics approach is complementary to the NHST approach (Calin-Jageman and Cumming, 2019).
source: As articulated in the work of Calin-Jageman and Cumming (Calin-Jageman and Cumming, 2019), the Estimation Statistics approach is complementary to the NHST approach, and provides a principled way to measure effect sizes coupled with estimates of uncertainty, yielding interval estimates of effect size.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Calin-Jageman and Cumming, 2019.

claim: The Estimation Statistics approach provides a principled way to measure effect sizes coupled with estimates of uncertainty, yielding interval estimates of effect size.
source: As articulated in the work of Calin-Jageman and Cumming (Calin-Jageman and Cumming, 2019), the Estimation Statistics approach is complementary to the NHST approach, and provides a principled way to measure effect sizes coupled with estimates of uncertainty, yielding interval estimates of effect size.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Calin-Jageman and Cumming, 2019, describing the properties of the Estimation Statistics approach.

claim: A false-alarm was defined as a trial on which the monkey made an eye-movement to a non-target stimulus at the cued location, within the same time window, relative to stimulus onset, that was applied to targets when detecting hits.
source: We defined a false-alarm as a trial on which the monkey made an eye-movement to a non-target stimulus at the cued location, within the same time window, relative to stimulus onset, that was applied to targets when detecting hits.
evidence: The claim describes the operational definition used in the data analysis.

claim: There was no difference in FA rates across laser and no-laser conditions.
source: There was no difference in FA rates across laser and no-laser conditions, so FA rates were averaged across these conditions, below.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of false alarm rates between experimental conditions in the data.

claim: Maximum likelihood fits were obtained for 20 jackknives of the data with 5% of trials left out for each jackknife.
source: For each of these five approaches, we obtained the maximum likelihood fits to 20 jackknives of the corresponding data (with 5% of trials left out for each jackknife).
evidence: The claim describes the statistical method (jackknife resampling) applied to the data.

claim: The threshold value for each experimental condition was taken as the average across the 20 jackknife fits.
source: The threshold value for each experimental condition was taken as the average across the 20 jackknife fits.
evidence: The claim describes the method used to estimate threshold values from the jackknife analysis.

claim: FA rates were slightly but significantly higher when attention was directed toward the opsin site.
source: FA rates were slightly but significantly higher when attention was directed toward the opsin site, so FA rates were computed separately for each attention condition (attend to opsin site ['attend-in'], attend away from opsin site ['attend-away']).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical comparison of false alarm rates between attention conditions in the experimental data.

claim: Repeating the analyses by computing FA rates from trials collapsed across attention conditions did not materially change the result.
source: Repeating these analyses by computing FA rates from trials collapsed across attention conditions did not materially change the result.

claim: Over-constraining the fits can lead to erroneous estimates of threshold and slope (Wichmann and Hill, 2001).
source: To avoid over-constraining the fits and obtaining erroneous estimates of threshold and slope (Wichmann and Hill, 2001), we left the lapse rate as a free parameter during the fitting procedures.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wichmann and Hill, 2001.

claim: The lapse rate was left as a free parameter during the fitting procedures.
source: To avoid over-constraining the fits and obtaining erroneous estimates of threshold and slope (Wichmann and Hill, 2001), we left the lapse rate as a free parameter during the fitting procedures.
evidence: The claim describes a methodological choice made in the data analysis to avoid over-constraining fits.

claim: Less than 5% of the effect size distribution fell below zero for the attend-in condition for all fitting methods.
source: Less than 5% of the effect size distribution fell below zero for the attend-in condition for all fitting methods (Panel B), supporting the conclusion that low-frequency laser stimulation causes an impairment in orientation discrimination.
evidence: The claim is supported by the bootstrap sampling distributions shown in Panel B of the figure and the statistical analysis.

claim: Low-frequency laser stimulation causes an impairment in orientation discrimination.

claim: The 95% confidence intervals contain zero for the attend away condition for all fitting methods.
source: The 95% confidence intervals contain zero for the attend away condition for all fitting methods, providing no indication that low-frequency laser stimulation altered orientation discrimination at the non-opsin site.

claim: Low-frequency laser stimulation did not alter orientation discrimination at the non-opsin site.

claim: Induction of low-frequency correlations at the opsin site impairs orientation discrimination for stimuli appearing at the retinotopic location of the opsin site.
source: From these analyses, we conclude that induction of low-frequency correlations at the opsin site impairs orientation discrimination for stimuli appearing at the retinotopic location of the opsin site, and causes no measurable impairment at the non-opsin site.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of the estimation statistics analyses across five different fitting methods.

claim: Induction of low-frequency correlations causes no measurable impairment at the non-opsin site.
source: From these analyses, we conclude that induction of low-frequency correlations at the opsin site impairs orientation discrimination for stimuli appearing at the retinotopic location of the opsin site, and causes no measurable impairment at the non-opsin site.

claim: The finding that low-frequency correlations impair orientation discrimination holds across five different approaches to treating FA rates.
source: This finding holds across five different approaches to treating FA rates.
evidence: The claim is based on the consistency of results across five different analytical methods for computing false alarm rates.

claim: There is compelling evidence for an impairment at the opsin site.
source: Thus, while we do find compelling evidence for an impairment at the opsin site, the evidence is mixed as to whether this impairment is entirely limited to that site.
